“We’ve been baptized in fire” – the new Rainbow Six boss on losing staff, Tencent, GTA and… Moana
Why a new-look Rainbow Six team is looking to its past
Christopher Dring
Sep 22, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Ubisoft’s Josh Mills on…
The trials of Siege X
Life under Tencent
Younger vs older players
Siege 2
You would imagine there is little to connect gritty tactical shooter Rainbow Six: Siege with animated Disney movie Moana. But you’d be surprised.
During a talk at one of Ubisoft’s developer conferences, Siege creative director Joshua Mills showed a clip from the movie where the lead character triumphantly sings: “I am Moana.”
The moment happens after Moana’s failed attempt to return a magical gem. She’s left adrift in the ocean feeling defeated, abandoned and lost. Until a ghost from her past appears, reminds her of who she is, and gives her the strength to fight again.
It’s that energy Mills is trying to bring to his tenure as the head of Siege.
Last year, the development team delivered the X update to mark ten years of the shooter. It introduced a free tier, a new mode, countless quality of life features, modernized visuals, destructible items and more. It was a hugely ambitious undertaking that didn’t go entirely to plan.
“There’s a ridiculous amount of technical risk in doing something like that,” says Mills in today’s The Game Business Show .
“We were essentially building a game while still shipping the live game at the same time for a good while. You’re ripping parts of the engine out and putting new parts in. It was a huge undertaking. A lot of fatigue was building on the team.
“As soon as we launched, we needed to rest. We had to give the team time to recover, and that caused a content lull in the seasonal cadence. That really hurt because people were super excited about all the changes and the future of Siege, and then we went a little quiet. We misaligned with the expectations of our community, and we had some trust to rebuild after that.”
That exhaustion brought about change in the team, too. And not just for Mills, who took over from Alexander Karpazis earlier this year.
“A lot of them had been on the project for seven years or longer,” Mills explains. “Many felt that Siege X was a big moment to finish that chapter before moving on.
“There was a big shift in personnel. Obviously, there are growing pains that come with everyone adjusting into new roles. But there’s this constant evolution where people bring their best for a bunch of years, put what they can into the game, and then move on.”
Mills was faced with a tired team that needed rebuilding, but the pain didn’t stop there. In December 2025, Rainbow Six: Siege was targeted by a hacker group that forced Ubisoft to take the game offline. The security breach saw thousands of accounts banned and unbanned and gave players large sums of in-game currency.
“Let’s just say I didn’t have hair before this, so it’s not like I lost it during the process,” he jokes.
“Honestly, the new core team has become very good friends. We’ve been baptized in the fire of everything going on, and it feels like we can handle anything together. As things come up, we take our hits, figure out what to do, and keep moving. Whether a new cheat provider comes out and attacks the game, we get on it.”
Much like Moana, the new Rainbow Six team is looking to its past as it moves forward.
“A few years ago, we had a real tone shift in the game,” Mills tells us.
‘The last Six Invitational [esports event] we did in Montreal where [in-game character] Harry was killed by Deimos - this is all lore stuff in a PVP game and I know that doesn’t necessarily shake everyone - but when it happened, it was a real signal that the stakes are back and Rainbow Six is back. We’re going to be that counter-terrorist unit. We’re going to have this gritty and grounded approach, because it was a little combat sports-esque before that.
“We’re doubling down on this and focusing on that back-to-roots.”
You can check out the full chat with Mills above. Or, alternatively, read on for some other key stories.
Sponsored Message
Scale globally. Keep quality in control
Keywords Studios is the games industry’s end-to-end partner, with 13,000 people across 26 countries helping studios build, launch and support games at global scale. Supercharged by technology and shaped by long-term partnership, Keywords Studios connects specialist expertise around the player experience.
For global impact, that means helping studios prepare games for more markets, languages, platforms and launch windows while keeping quality, context and control where they matter most. From localisation planning and QA to LQA and launch support, Keywords Studios helps protect meaning, tone and release quality at global scale.
New Ubisoft structure is ‘a really good improvement’
Vantage Studios oversees Far Cry, Assassin’s Creed and Rainbow Six
Last year, Rainbow Six Siege was moved under a new division within Ubisoft called Vantage Studios. Led by Charlie Guillemot and Christophe Derennes, Vantage Studios is 26% owned by Tencent, which invested €1.16 billion in the division.
And according to Mills, it has had an immediate impact.
“Things have definitely changed. One of the coolest things is that we have a more direct line with HQ. When the hack happened at Christmas, Charlie and I were figuring out what was going on and calling people in. We were all in it together, thick as thieves. There was a real rally point around the game to protect it.
“If there are conversations or resources we need, we can just talk. There are fewer layers to go through to have a transparent conversation, which is a really good improvement.
“Outside of that, regarding Tencent, we’re definitely working with [them]. We’ve announced Siege China, and that’s been a great collaboration. There’s a lot of insight on that region that we don’t have.”
Rainbow Six: Siege has some surprises planned for GTA 6 launch
If you, like me, spend time poring over player numbers, you’ll know that whenever a big title comes out, it often has a negative effect on the games around it.
According to Ampere, across October and November, Rainbow Six Siege lost millions of players to titles like Battlefield 6, Call of Duty: Black Ops 7 and Arc Raiders.
Mills says the key is to look after the players who stick around.
“We’ve got a massive launch coming with GTA,” Mills observes. “It doesn’t matter what genre you’re in; you’re going to take a hit when that drops. People are going to play it, and then they’ll come back. Heck, all of us are going to play it.
“It’s about being smart with your expectations so you can keep the team and HQ aligned. If the team sees player numbers dip, they can get anxious, but it’s generally temporary.
“Our golden rule is to serve the players who stay like kings and queens. We don’t go on vacation just because a competitor is swelling the market. We double down and reward those spending their valuable time with us.”
But surely they don’t plan to do any major updates when GTA 6 drops?
“Funnily enough, Season Four will drop right around that time,” Mills says. “That shifts up the game in different ways. We actually have some unannounced surprises held back to make a splash.”
Siege’s audience has shifted younger
It may be 11 years-old, but Rainbow Six: Siege has seen its audience skew younger. And that has created a challenge.
“Their expectations are different,” says Mills.
“Someone who played 10 years ago, like myself, isn’t going to be the most mechanically driven player anymore. I have to rely on strategy and gadgets. A lot of younger players are insane with their sticks or keyboard and mouse, so they run and gun a bit more, which changes the pace and meta of the game.
“Even with the market shifting younger, we remind ourselves that Siege is a tactical, methodical game. We need to stay true to that. Anytime we’ve veered away, we get immediate backlash from the core. This is a thinking man’s shooter. It’s chess at its core.
“In the past, we’ve slowed down aim-down-sights times, because players were so mechanically good they were breaking the netcode with how fast they moved and jiggle-peeked [a tactical strafing technique used in shooters]. When that happens, it breaks the immersion of being an elite tactical unit and makes you look like Rambo. If you want to wall-run and swan dive, Siege isn’t the place for you.”
Ubisoft recruits pro players to test Siege
Ubisoft tests all Rainbow Six: Siege updates with professional esports players.
“They’re going to be the ones who will break it very fast,” Mills says. “They’re like, ‘If you do this, then the game is unplayable for these reasons.’ So, we work closely with our pro teams to have really early testing. At this point, they’re usually two or three operators [playable characters] ahead of where we actually are in the release calendar.
“We’ll go to a major, which is one of our esports events, and we’ll show the pros everything for the reveal coming up, and things coming down the line, to get their feedback on whether it aligns to what they expect at their level.”
There’s no need for a Siege 2
As the game approaches its eleventh year, questions are being asked as to whether it’s time for a whole new Siege game. Mills isn’t convinced.
“It came up a lot during the X update,” he says. “The question was, ‘Why do Siege X and not just do Siege 2?’ Fundamentally rebuilding our entire system is a mountain of work. Siege X is not even close to the level of scale we’re talking about if we were to go and rebuild the entire game.
“End of the day, the way we’ve architectured our technology is very modular. So, when we did X, we rebuilt the audio and the lighting system, and both of those are maturing right now. The foundations were rebuilt. So, the need for doing it is not necessarily there with the cost of shutting the lights off. Because you can’t possibly run both at the same time. You would need the expertise of the team that’s running the game to rebuild it. It’d be really difficult to do.”
What’s more, for a lot of modern games, players don’t seem too concerned with visual fidelity.
“I was at the Esports World Cup in Paris, and we had the demo booth set up with the new season. Every time I walked by, all the screens were set by four-by-three and stretched resolution. Everything was on low, because everyone’s going for all those [frames per second]. The core audience of Siege runs like this. When we were rebuilding the lighting and modernizing the maps, it was: Should we really do this? Does anybody care?”
“The richness is what everybody has in their head with Rainbow Six. They think of the original E3 trailer. They think of flashlights and gritty and people rappelling down the building and breaking in. Whereas in the game, because we were so focused on competitive, we had cleaned all that out and made everything super readable.”
However, realism is important to players, Mills concludes. Just not necessarily in the visual sense.
“We had these gas pipes. We showed them for the first time. And one of the pro teams said, ‘you can’t put those on the Bank map.’ We’re like, ‘why?’ ‘Well, gas pipes wouldn’t be in a bank… maybe in the basement.’ They cared more about the realization of it being in the basement. And I’m like, ‘You’re the same players who will turn off everything and stretch the resolution’. But they care that the gas pipes make sense.”
Check out the full interview with Mills above.

title: Halo to Activision. Xbox merges studios and cuts 268 jobs
author: Christopher Dring
excerpt: Rare, Obsidian, World’s Edge have new homes. Ninja Theory faces closure
text:
Discover more from The Game Business
Expert analysis, exclusive data, and in-depth interviews on the global video game industry — delivered by industry insider Christopher Dring.
Already have an account? Sign in
Halo to Activision. Xbox merges studios and cuts 268 jobs
Rare, Obsidian, World’s Edge have new homes. Ninja Theory faces closure
Christopher Dring
Sep 22, 2026
Xbox has reorganized its studio business, with several developers now reporting into either Bethesda or Activision Blizzard.
Meanwhile, Hellblade developer Ninja Theory faces closure after two buyout talks fell through.
Halo will now be entirely led by Call of Duty publisher Activision. Halo Studios will continue to support existing in-market projects, while a new purpose-built team will make the next Halo game.
Sea of Thieves developer Rare and Age of Empires division World’s Edge will also report to Activision.
Developer Obsidian will report directly to Bethesda. Obsidian is already working on a new Fallout game for the publisher.
Forza Motorsport developer Turn10 will be folded into Forza Horizon studio Playground Games.
Undead Labs will now become an independent studio, with an unnamed publisher handling the release of State of Decay 3. The game will continue to be released in Game Pass on day one.
Finally, Microsoft’s casual games division will report into Candy Crush company King.
As a result of these changes, there will be 268 job cuts across Halo Studios, other first-party teams and the Xbox Game Studios central organization.
“We’re thrilled to welcome Halo, Rare, and World’s Edge to Activision,” said Activision president Rob Kostich. “It’s an honor and a responsibility that we do not take lightly.  These teams and their games have inspired fans around the world for decades.
“For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place.  It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community.
“To the World’s Edge and Rare teams, we can’t wait to get to work together.”
Xbox Chief Creative Officer Matt Booty said: “The goal is to strengthen our franchises and games by operating fewer business units, aligning groups that already work closely together, and focusing our publishing expertise.”
Xbox announced it would cut 3,200 jobs as part of a major restructure in July. This included the removal of five studios. Double Fine (Keeper), Compulsion Games (South of Midnight, Ninja Theory (Hellblade), Undead Labs (State of Decay) and Arkane Lyon (Dishonored).
The Arkane process is on-going and expected to continue until the end of 2026.
The company says it is three quarters of the way through its planned restructure.
The initial wave of 1,600 job cuts included job losses at Obsidian, Bethesda and id Software, alongside significant reductions across the Xbox platform team, which covers hardware, software services, xCloud and Game Pass.
Xbox says the job cuts will allow it to invest in other areas. It has already signed ambitious new IP Physint from Kojima Productions.

title: The Unsung Indie Heroes of Steam: Four Paths to a Sustainable Indie Career
author: Jennie Burton
text:
The Unsung Indie Heroes of Steam: Four Paths to a Sustainable Indie Career

Author: Jennie Burton, Head of Marketing
Category: Guides & Tips
Published: 9/22/2026
Updated: 9/7/2026
When people picture a successful indie game developer, they tend to imagine the outliers: the overnight hit
the viral trailer
the game that sells millions of copies and turns its creator into the industry’s next household name.
This is just one version of success.
Between the blockbuster successes and the projects that earn almost nothing is a much larger, less visible group of developers quietly building sustainable careers. They may not dominate headlines or appear in every “Top Indie Games” list, but their games earn enough to fund the next project, or eventually make full-time development possible.
Games such as The Ouroboros King , 3dSen , Execute , and Master of Chess sit in that middle ground. Each earned its developers more than $160,000 in gross revenue, despite being made by solo developers or very small teams. The best thing is you’ve probably never heard of them.
Our analysis found more than 300 Steam games with estimated gross revenue of roughly $160,000 to $890,000. Once Steam’s fee, taxes, development costs, and other expenses are accounted for, that range can represent something close to an average US salary of around $70,000. It’s not a guaranteed route to wealth, and gross revenue is not personal income, but it’s a useful reminder that an indie career does not have to be all-or-nothing.
The developers below took very different routes:
One leveraged a data-science background to make focused, achievable projects.
One spent a decade on an unusual technical passion project.
One used a smaller release to recover from burnout and build momentum towards a dream game.
One spent years making games alongside a conventional software job before finding commercial success.
Their stories point to a more realistic and encouraging picture of what an indie game career can look like.
1. Oriol Cosp: Turning Data Skills Into Game Development
Leaving a secure, well-paid tech job for indie development can sound like a lottery-ticket gamble, but Oriol Cosp’s experience suggests that it doesn’t have to be.
Cosp made his first game, The Ouroboros King , while working full-time as a data scientist and raising a young child. He brought eight years of coding experience to the project and deliberately selected an idea that was both technically approachable and aligned with familiar player expectations.
His goal was to do for chess what Slay the Spire had done for card games; use an established foundation, combine it with roguelike progression and strategic variation, and create something recognisable but distinct. The concept reduced his need for extensive art production while allowing him to focus on systems, programming, and game design.
Time was not a commodity here.. Cosp reportedly committed around three to four hours a day, five days a week, and later used vacation time to accelerate development. He released a prototype on itch.io in June 2022, followed with a Steam demo, and committed early to a February 2023 full release.
The Ouroboros King launched on 27 February 2023. Cosp’s own sales expectations were modest: he anticipated making a little over $1,000. Instead, the game sold more than 5,000 copies in its first month!
In a blog post a year later, he estimated he’d made around $84,000 in profit after costs, including an allowance for his own time. For him, that made the move from data science to full-time indie development financially credible.
His second game, Gods vs Horrors , performed less strongly, but the important part of his story is what happened next. He documented the lessons, continued learning, and moved forward with further releases rather than treating one weaker result as a verdict on his career.
What developers can learn
Price your own time - It’s easy to treat nights, weekends, and self-directed work as free. Early on, that may be unavoidable, but a sustainable career requires acknowledging that your time is valuable.
Choose designs that match your constraints - Cosp didn’t start with a game that demanded a huge art team, a vast world, or years of content production. He found a concept that made practical use of his strongest skills.
Borrow familiar patterns, then recombine them - Players who understand Slay the Spire, chess, or autobattler-style strategy have a lower learning barrier when encountering a new game built from similar ideas.
Treat every launch as an experiment - Cosp’s detailed post-mortems turn releases into compounding experience. A project’s commercial result matters, but so does what it teaches about development, marketing, scope, and audience.

2. Geod Studios: The Decade-Long Passion Project
The next route couldn’t be more different.
Geod Studios spent around 10 years creating 3dSen , a 3D NES emulator that reimagines classic Nintendo Entertainment System games in three dimensions. What began as a hobby project that was expected to take roughly a year eventually became a decade-long technical undertaking.
The VR version entered Early Access in 2019 with 46 supported games. The PC version followed in 2020 with 70. By the time of the final build, more than 100 games had been individually supported and built by Geod.
The scale of that work becomes clearer when you consider the original goal; Geod initially hoped that an algorithm could automate the conversion of NES games into 3D. In practice, the algorithm only worked around half the time, but instead of abandoning the project, he adjusted the plan.
He developed a four-step pipeline combining automation with manual work. Simpler games, such as Donkey Kong , could take a few days to build and more complicated titles, such as The Legend of Zelda , could take months.
That compromise was crucial. A fully automatic process would have been elegant, but it wasn’t workable. By accepting a hybrid workflow, Geod kept moving towards the experience he wanted to create; revisiting favourite childhood games in 3D.
The project also accumulated attention over time. The Early Access releases intrigued journalists, while the ongoing work created a reason for interested players to follow the project’s progress. 3dSen PC alone has sold around 27,000 copies since launching in 2025. It has also developed a small but dedicated community around 3dSen Maker , where users create and upload their own 3D versions of NES games. One community member has uploaded more than a dozen completed games.
Across both versions, 3dSen has generated roughly $600,000 in gross revenue. Spread over 10 years and reduced by platform fees, taxes, and expenses, that’s not a shortcut to a fortune, but it is a meaningful payoff for an unusually focused and enduring project.
What Developer's Can Learn
A compromise can save a project - Geod did not get the fully automated process he originally wanted, but by changing the production method instead of abandoning the goal, he found a path to completion.
Technical niches can be commercially valuable - A 3D NES emulator is not a broad, mass-market premise, but it serves a specific curiosity and a specific community exceptionally well.
Progress itself can be marketing - Long-running projects can give players, journalists, and niche communities something meaningful to follow. The work becomes part of the story.
3. Payne Robinson: A Smaller Game as a Pivot
Payne Robinson demonstrates another route: learning game development from scratch while holding a job in an entirely different field.
Robinson is a full-time English teacher who taught himself game development in Godot. His original project, Grid Tweaker , remains his larger dream game, but it had a large scope and balancing that ambition with a full-time job made the learning curve steep and progress slow.
Eventually, he burned out.
Rather than cancel Grid Tweaker or force himself to keep working on something that had become overwhelming, Robinson switched to a smaller idea. The result was Execute , a project he completed in roughly six to nine months.
That decision did more than create a break from a difficult project. It gave him a way to regain enthusiasm, practise shipping, and build systems and skills that could later support work on Grid Tweaker . Small pieces of time at lunch and after work became meaningful because they were being invested in a project with a nearer finish line.
Execute generated around $206,000 in gross revenue, enough for Robinson to pay off his student loan. He’s also spoken about using a portfolio of commercial releases as a route towards eventually working full-time on his dream game.
His story is especially useful for developers who are still learning, who work outside the game industry, or who feel trapped by the size of their first ambitious idea. It is possible to keep the dream project alive without insisting that it must be your first commercial release.
What developers can learn
Your first game does not need to be your dream game - A smaller project can build confidence, skills, reusable systems, and an audience without demanding years of all-or-nothing effort.
A pause is not a failure - Switching projects can be the healthy choice when burnout is undermining progress. The key is to choose a smaller project that still contributes to your longer-term ambitions.
Small, consistent time blocks add up - Lunch breaks and evenings may not be enough for a huge production, but they can be enough to ship a tightly scoped game.
Transferable skills matter - Robinson’s teaching background also supports his YouTube work, where he explains his process in an entertaining and accessible way. A previous career can provide advantages rather than being irrelevant baggage.
4. Brane: Building Commercial Success Alongside a Day Job
Brane offers yet another view of game development; developing games alongside a conventional software career for more than a decade before finding commercial success.
He’d been experimenting with game development for years while becoming increasingly dissatisfied with his software-development day job. In effect, he was moonlighting as a game developer. His first commercial breakthrough came with Master of Chess , released in September 2025.
Like Cosp and Robinson, Brane has embraced a habit of shipping smaller projects and learning through release. But his early approach differed in that many of those projects were free-to-play.
Since 2017, he’s released small-scope games on itch.io, including the memorably named I Have No Hands and I Must Hug . Even his Steam release before Master of Chess was free.
Releasing free games is not the only or necessarily the best route though because developers deserve to be paid for their work, but free releases can remove the pressure of expecting a financial return from every experiment. For a developer with an alternative stable income, that can create room to practice, explore, and improve without attaching every creative decision to a sales forecast.
Brane’s other strength was commitment to an unusually specific niche. He describes Master of Chess as a niche game and didn’t expect it to perform as well as it did, yet its premise as a chess equivalent of Football Manager gave it a powerful identity. It wasn’t trying to appeal to everyone, it was attempting to delight people intensely interested in the intersection of chess and management simulation.
That focus helped attract dedicated fans. Brane built a Discord community of more than 1,000 members and posted development updates there every day, all while working full-time and becoming a father for the first time.
Master of Chess earned around $290,000 in gross Steam revenue and he then released another commercial game, Confidential Killings , with designer Lorenzo. That game performed even better, earning approximately $270,000 in gross revenue for each collaborator.
What developers can learn
Stable employment can be an asset - A job can reduce financial pressure, and make it possible to experiment without needing every game to pay the bills immediately.
Free projects can be deliberate practice - When used intentionally, they can help developers learn shipping, feedback, production, and audience-building before commercial stakes are added.
Niche is not the same as small opportunity - A clear, distinctive promise can attract deeply invested players who have few alternatives designed specifically for them.
Build a community around the obsession - Brane’s frequent Discord updates made his commitment visible. People often follow sustained enthusiasm before they decide to buy the finished game.
What These Four Stories Have in Common
These developers made different kinds of games, had different professional backgrounds, and worked on radically different timelines, yet their stories share several important patterns.
Pattern
What it looked like in practice
They kept a financial foundation
None of them went full-time before their first game made it financially viable, and some continue to work conventional jobs.
They worked within constraints
Time, family responsibilities, technical skills, limited art capacity, and available income shaped their project choices.
They committed to distinct niches
Chess roguelikes, 3D NES games, compact programming-inspired puzzle games, and chess management are specific propositions rather than generic ones.
They built in public to some degree
Blogs, Steam demos, Early Access, YouTube, Discord, and ongoing development updates gave audiences reasons to pay attention.
They learned through releases
Their careers were not built on a single flawless plan. They adapted with prototypes, free games, smaller releases, setbacks, and post-mortems.
They found a way to continue
Each developer made compromises that kept game development compatible with their actual life.
The point is not that every developer should make a chess game, spend 10 years on one project, quit their day job, or release free games.
It’s that successful indie development often looks more ordinary than the stories that dominate the media. It can be gradual. It can be niche. It can happen alongside a job. It can start with a small project rather than a dream project. It can involve setbacks, compromises, detours, and years of learning.
And it can still be a real success.
A More Sustainable Definition of Success
The game industry often presents developers with a false binary: either make a viral smash hit or disappear without a trace. There’s a broad spectrum between those two extremes.
For many developers, a sustainable goal might be to earn enough to finance the next game, pay down debt, build a portfolio, grow a community, reduce dependence on a day job, or eventually transition to full-time development when the numbers support it.
The developers in this article all continued because they found ways to make the work meaningful enough to sustain. They designed around the lives they actually had, rather than waiting for perfect conditions. They found niches they cared about, shipped work, learned from it, and allowed their experience to compound.
If you’re developing a game alongside a job, feeling overwhelmed by a large project, or worrying that a non-viral launch means the end of the road, these stories are a useful reminder that your path may not resemble the biggest success stories in indie games. And it doesn’t need to!
A sustainable indie career can be built in the middle.
